terminal.description: The screen runs in the Browser panel and reloads every time you save. This shell opens in your workspace in case you want to look around.

tasks.title: Put App on the screen
tasks.description:
`src/main.jsx` is the script `index.html` loads. Make it draw the `App` component from `src/App.jsx` inside the element with the id `root`.

When it works, the Browser panel shows the museum's name.

The check swaps in an `App` of its own and looks for what it draws inside `#root`.
nextSteps: Read "Putting it on the screen" in the lesson.
Make a root on the element with the id `root`.
Render `App` into it, save, and look at the Browser panel.
hints: Open `index.html` and find the one element React should draw into.
`createRoot` takes an element of the page and gives back a root. A root has a `render` method that takes what to draw.
React wants an element, so the component goes to `render` written as a tag: `<App />`, not `App`.

tasks.title: Write the OpeningHours component
tasks.description:
Below `App` in `src/App.jsx`, write a component called `OpeningHours` and export it by name. It returns: - a `
` with the class `hours` - inside it, an `

` that reads `Opening hours` - and a `

` that reads `Every day, 10:00 to 16:00` The check draws `OpeningHours` on its own and reads what it returns. React's warnings count too: a class written the HTML way fails the task.
nextSteps: Read "A component is a function that returns markup" in the lesson.
Write an exported function named `OpeningHours`, with a capital O and a capital H.
Return the section with its heading and its line.
Look at the console in the Browser panel: it should show no warning.
hints: A component is a plain function. Its name, its `export` and its `return` work like any other function.
The markup is HTML with JSX's names for attributes. Look at how `App` gives the outer `div` its class.
The function returns one `section` element with the `className` `hours`; the `h2` and the `p` sit inside it.

tasks.title: Show the opening hours in App
tasks.description:
Make `App` show your `OpeningHours` under the heading, by using it as a tag. Keep the heading and the footer where they are.

The check draws `App` and looks for the opening hours under the heading. It also asks React which component drew them, so markup copied into `App` does not count.
nextSteps: Read "Components inside components" in the lesson.
Find the heading in what `App` returns.
Use `OpeningHours` on the line below it.
Save and look at the Browser panel.
hints: A component you wrote is used in JSX the same way as an HTML element.
The tag is the component's name, exactly as you wrote it, capital letters included.

tasks.title: Two lines in the footer
tasks.description:
Below `OpeningHours`, write a component called `FooterLines` and export it by name. It returns two paragraphs, in this order:

- `Foundry Lane, Coalbrook`
- `Run by volunteers since 1987`

Nothing wraps them: no `div`, no other element. Then show `FooterLines` inside the `footer` that `App` already has.

The check draws `FooterLines` on its own and expects exactly the two paragraphs, with no warning from React. Then it draws `App` and looks inside the footer.
nextSteps: Read "One element comes back" in the lesson.
If the page stops loading, read the bundler's message in the Browser panel's console.
hints: A function gives back one value. Two elements next to each other are two values.
There is a way to group elements that adds nothing to the page. It looks like a tag with no name.
Wrap the two paragraphs in `<>` and `</>`, then put `<FooterLines />` between the footer's tags.
